read_from: The route text as served, in the extract this reissue counts (scratch/routes-merged-v1.2/stepbible_tbesh_gloss.jsonl): the 2,645 rows of this source in the route store as served on 7 November 2026 AD (store_version 3d8c4ef86c01 at main 1d2470eb356b, 652,885 routes in all), followed by the 198 records of this source in the span store as served (schema span-store-served-v1, from span-store-v2.1, dictionary store cc890b8a7992, ledgers applied on 2026-11-07; 1,698 records in all, axis: records), each a name or a phrase of two or more Hebrew words read as one, with its own route text, which the classifier reads like any route; a span record is one JSON per line with key, route, def, m, year and cut, and the span store's own fields, which are not marks. The figures of this field count that extract (2,843 routes, axis: routes) except where they name the source audit of the shipped ledger, which covers the route store's rows only; the span store's records were not audited against the source here. For the route store's rows, which are byte for byte the rows the shipped ledger read: the route text as served: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4 (its index.json), for "STEP Bible Translators Brief Lexicon Hebrew scholar-created Gloss column" (M19): 2,843 routes (axis: routes), 2,001 letters keys (axis: keys). The definition field of the same row equals the route text on 2,843 of the routes. The source audit (builder/02-audit.mjs, builder/02b-audit-more.mjs; evidence about the source and no part of any test): the source is the TBESH file in the lane's copy of STEPBible-Data, ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/stepbible-data-2026-07-14/Lexicons/. Each of the dictionary store's 2,870 records names one line of that file, and its text equals that line's Gloss column on 2,870; its two other text fields are filled on 0 and 0 records. 2,645 of the 2,645 routes tie to a record of the same text, with runs of white space closed up and the ends trimmed as the served text has them, and a Hebrew headword of the same letters. By the file's own lines, 2,595 routes stand on one line and 50 on two or more lines that give the same text; by the store's records, 2,618 tie to one record and 27 to two or more (axis: routes, both). So a route comes from one column, and no test here stands on a guess about a field. The file's Meaning column asks for permission, is not served, and was neither kept nor read for this. The source's own key: the head of the file (the 52 lines before its header line) is on file and was read whole. It describes the fields: of the Gloss it says only who made it, and of the disambiguated numbers that they set apart distinct sub-meanings of words and distinct individuals of one name. No line of it names a colon, a slash, a bracket, a comma, a hyphen or a grave accent, and neither does a line that names this source in the README at the top of the copy or in the 27 of the 579 files of the works-own-stamp folder that name it (builder/05-key-search.mjs, source-audit/key-search.json). The notes at the head of the sister file TAHOT give a key to that file's own English column, where a slash mirrors the parts of a Hebrew word, words in angle brackets are best not included in a translation and words in square brackets are implied. That is another column of another file and no key to this one: a slash here does not mirror parts of a word, and no angle bracket stands here. It bears here twice. TAHOT writes the word of the row with the label as an angle-bracket word, which is why that row has its own question. And TAHOT's tags split this dictionary's colon rows at the colon, second part first (the tag of the row belly: abdomen reads ": abdomen»belly:1_abdomen"): 566 of the 580 rows with a colon have such a tag under their own number, 526 exactly and 40 keeping one part (builder/02c-tahot-tags.mjs, source-audit/tahot-tags.json). The head of TAHOT (its lines 50 and 51) says a tag carries an English gloss and its sub-meaning after the sign », and gives a name for its example. Those words name the tag's parts and not this colon, and what follows the sign in the tag begins with this row's first part, so they do not name the colon's two parts. So the tags back the reading of the colon, the first part for the word and the second for what this row takes it to mean, and no more, and the colon shapes begin "unverified:", as every shape's meaning here does.

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one Unicode code point (every route that holds a mark here holds only characters of 16 bits, so a code point is one index of the JavaScript string). A letter is any character of Unicode category L (JavaScript \p{L}), of any script and in either case. A space is the character U+0020 only. No test asks for a digit, for whitespace, or for uppercase or lowercase as a class. Nothing is trimmed: the text is the whole route text as it stands, which is the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def; the text before and the text after the mark are the template's c.before and c.after. Empty means that the named text has no character at all, as at the start or the end of the route. Directly before and directly after name the one character next to the mark; where the mark stands at that end of the text no character stands there, so a test that asks for a character there fails. The whole text, exactly, means that the text equals the named string character for character. Holds means that at least one character of the named text is the named character, wherever it stands. Sits inside round brackets means that the template's c.container is paren for the mark. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it, and a full stop after » belongs to the sentence and not to the string. The apostrophe in every string is the straight one, U+0027. Every string and every list minds case and is matched exact to the character. No test uses the words begins with or contains.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. A test says not caught above where it takes what the shapes above it for the same mark did not take. Only the shape's test decides: the container field is not part of a test unless the test says sits inside round brackets, and the checker compares the field afterwards. An occurrence that no shape of its mark takes makes the classifier throw, and none does.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no number. The source's own file does, on every line (its eStrong and dStrong numbers, the first two columns), and the store dropped them from the route text, so a number cannot be read from a route. A letters key's texts are the glosses of every line spelt with those letters. Of the 373 keys with more than one text (axis: keys), the rows of 117 tie to one eStrong number, so their texts are meanings of one word, and the rows of 256 tie to two or more numbers, so they hold homonyms or other words of one spelling (example key שער: 7 texts, 7 numbers).

branches.question: Many rows hold two parts with a colon between them: to set: make. The first part names the word. The second part says what this row takes the word to mean. The page prints such a row today as one pill, as written, and goes on doing so until you rule. You can keep that one pill, print a pill for each part, or print a pill for the second part alone. Which? A short list, picked by hand, prints as written under every answer: rows whose second part repeats the first (to give: give), waits for the next word (son: type of) or is a bare small word (hand: by). Rows near them (rule: to rule, house: inside) stay in this question.

options.means: One pill with both parts, as written, as today: to set: make.

A pill for each part: to set and make. A row with a slash as well is cut at the colon and at the slash, whatever you rule for rows with a slash and no colon: land: country/planet prints land, country and planet. The same piece then stands on several rows of one card; the page folds an exact repeat on a card, so such a piece prints once.

A pill for the second part alone: to set: make prints make. This needs one step of the page's own, because a declaration's pieces must keep every character of the row; until then the row prints as written. It stays in the store as it is. What you give up: where this dictionary gives the word's plain gloss nowhere else on the card, that gloss leaves the card. A second part in square brackets prints with them (to make: [do] prints [do]), and one with a slash prints as written (land: country/planet prints country/planet). The rows on the short list keep both parts: son: type of.

branches.question: Some rows hold two or three parts with a slash between them and no colon: rain/teacher. Each part can stand alone, and nothing in the row says whether its parts are one meaning said twice or different meanings. Should the page print each part as its own pill? They print as one pill, as written, until you rule.

options.means: One pill, as written, as today: rain/teacher.
A pill for each part: rain and teacher. The page cuts at the slash and nowhere else.
